module_title: Ray Optics Basics & Huygens' Principle (Detailed Foundational)
introduction: This foundational level bridges the behavior of light as both a straight-line ray (Geometrical Optics) and a propagating wavefront (Physical Optics). It thoroughly covers the mechanics of reflection, the laws of refraction, Total Internal Reflection (TIR), and the foundational Lens Maker's formula.

core_concepts.title: Reflection and Spherical Mirrors
core_concepts.description: Reflection follows two laws: Angle of incidence equals angle of reflection ($\angle i = \angle r$), and the incident ray, reflected ray, and normal lie in the same plane. For spherical mirrors (Concave and Convex), the focal length is half the radius of curvature ($f = R/2$ for paraxial rays). The Mirror Formula connecting object distance ($u$), image distance ($v$), and focal length ($f$) is $\frac{1}{v} + \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$. Lateral magnification is $m = -\frac{v}{u}$.

core_concepts.title: Refraction and Snell's Law
core_concepts.description: Refraction is the bending of light when transitioning between media of different optical densities. Snell's Law states the ratio of the sine of the angle of incidence to the sine of the angle of refraction is a constant, known as the relative refractive index: $^1\mu_2 = \frac{\sin i}{\sin r} = \frac{\mu_2}{\mu_1} = \frac{v_1}{v_2}$. Note that during refraction, the velocity and wavelength of light change, but its frequency ($f$) remains absolutely constant.

core_concepts.title: Total Internal Reflection (TIR)
core_concepts.description: When light travels from a denser medium to a rarer medium and the angle of incidence exceeds a specific 'Critical Angle' ($i_c$), the light does not refract into the rarer medium but is entirely reflected back into the denser medium. The critical angle is given by $\sin i_c = \frac{\mu_{\text{rarer}}}{\mu_{\text{denser}}}$. This principle is the operational basis of optical fibers, diamond sparkling, and mirages.

core_concepts.title: Lenses and Lens Maker's Formula
core_concepts.description: A lens focuses or disperses light using refraction across two surfaces. The fundamental equation designing a lens is the Lens Maker's Formula: $\frac{1}{f} = (\mu_{rel} - 1) \left( \frac{1}{R_1} - \frac{1}{R_2} \right)$, where $\mu_{rel}$ is the refractive index of the lens relative to the surrounding medium. The Thin Lens Formula is $\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$ with lateral magnification $m = \frac{v}{u}$.

core_concepts.title: Huygens' Principle (Wave Nature)
core_concepts.description: Christiaan Huygens proposed that light travels as wavefronts (loci of points oscillating in the exact same phase). Principle: Every point on a primary wavefront acts as a source of secondary wavelets spreading out in all directions with the speed of light. The forward envelope of these wavelets forms the new wavefront. This elegantly proves both Snell's Law and the Laws of Reflection.

important_entities.name: Sign Convention (Cartesian System)
important_entities.key_fact: All distances are measured from the optical center / pole.
important_entities.significance: Distances measured in the direction of incident light are taken as POSITIVE ($+$), and those measured against it are NEGATIVE ($-$). For a real object, $u$ is universally negative. The focal length ($f$) of a converging lens/concave mirror is negative in some older conventions, but strictly POSITIVE for Convex Lenses/Mirrors and NEGATIVE for Concave Lenses/Mirrors in modern Cartesian conventions.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: If a convex glass lens ($\mu_g = 1.5$) is submerged in a liquid with a HIGHER refractive index (e.g., carbon disulfide, $\mu_l = 1.6$), the term $(\mu_{rel} - 1)$ in the Lens Maker's formula becomes negative. This means the Convex lens behaves physically as a Diverging (Concave) lens inside that liquid! If submerged in a liquid of EQUAL refractive index, it becomes invisible and acts like a plain glass sheet ($f = \infty$).

mnemonics_and_tricks.trick_title: Real is Inverted, Virtual is Erect
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: In single lens or single mirror systems, a Real image is always Inverted (magnification $m$ is negative), and a Virtual image is always Erect (magnification $m$ is positive).

exam_strategy_tips: In Apparent Depth problems, the apparent shift of an object viewed normally through a glass slab of thickness $t$ is $\Delta x = t \left( 1 - \frac{1}{\mu} \right)$. The shift is always in the direction of the incident light.
